Propagate 1D flat errors
_Issue [JP-3429](https://jira.stsci.edu/browse/JP-3429) was created on JIRA by [Melanie Clarke](https://jira.stsci.edu/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=mclarke):_

NIRSpec is updating its flat files to include a 1D error array, associated with the fast variation component in the F-flats (JP-3304).  The flat field step needs to be updated to propagate this error from the reference files to the output error arrays.

In particular, the combine_fast_slow function needs to be updated to take an error array as input and interpolate it onto the wavelengths for the observation.  The interpolated error should then be added in quadrature to any error from other components.

Two implementation notes:

1. Both zero and NaN are possible values for all flat error arrays, 2D and 1D.  The S and D flats will not have error arrays for their 1D components, so these values will default to NaN; their 2D error components will be set to zero, since all flat errors are accounted for in the F-flat instead. When combining flat error values, NaN values should be ignored and zero values should be treated as valid numbers.  

2. The 1D flat vector in the combine_fast_slow algorithm is interpolated with a 3-point Gaussian integration.  A rigorous error propagation through that step should take into account cross-correlations between the pixels that are weighted and summed together, but we don't recommend that.  The flat errors are not likely to be known to enough precision to justify the complexity.  Instead, we recommend interpolating the error vector onto the wavelengths with a simple linear interpolation, e.g.:
  error_value = np.interp(wavelengths, tab_wl, tab_flat_error, left=np.nan, right=np.nan)
</issue_description>

The issue is requesting implementation of **1D flat error propagation** in the JWST pipeline for NIRSpec instruments. Here's my understanding:

Currently, the flat field step doesn't propagate 1D error arrays from reference files to the output error arrays. NIRSpec is updating its flat files to include these 1D error arrays for the fast variation component in F-flats, and the pipeline needs to be updated to handle this properly.

1. Run flat field processing on NIRSpec data with updated F-flat reference files containing 1D error arrays
2. Observe that the 1D errors are not propagated to the output error arrays
3. Expected behavior: 1D errors should be interpolated and combined in quadrature with existing errors

### 1.5 Best Practices
- Handle NaN and zero values correctly according to specifications
- Use simple linear interpolation for errors (not Gaussian integration like flats)
- Combine errors in quadrature properly
- Maintain backward compatibility with existing reference files

    20	## Installation
    21	
    22	Please contact the [JWST Help Desk](https://jwsthelp.stsci.edu) for installation issues.
    23	
    24	The easiest way to install the latest `jwst` release into a fresh virtualenv or conda environment is
    25	
    26	    pip install jwst
    27	
    28	### Detailed Installation
    29	
    30	The `jwst` package can be installed into a virtualenv or conda environment via `pip`.
    31	We recommend that for each installation you start by creating a fresh
    32	environment that only has Python installed and then install the `jwst` package and
    33	its dependencies into that bare environment.
    34	If using conda environments, first make sure you have a recent version of Anaconda
    35	or Miniconda installed.
    36	If desired, you can create multiple environments to allow for switching between different
    37	versions of the `jwst` package (e.g. a released version versus the current development version).
    38	
    39	In all cases, the installation is generally a 3-step process:
    40	* Create a conda environment
    41	* Activate that environment
    42	* Install the desired version of the `jwst` package into that environment
    43	
    44	Details are given below on how to do this for different types of installations,
    45	including tagged releases, DMS builds used in operations, and development versions.
    46	Remember that all conda operations must be done from within a bash/zsh shell.
    47	
    48	
    49	### Installing latest releases
    50	
    51	You can install the latest released version via `pip`.  From a bash/zsh shell:
    52	
    53	    conda create -n <env_name> python
    54	    conda activate <env_name>
    55	    pip install jwst
    56	
    57	You can also install a specific version:
    58	
    59	    conda create -n <env_name> python
    60	    conda activate <env_name>
    61	    pip install jwst==1.9.4
    62	
    63	### Installing the development version from Github
    64	
    65	You can install the latest development version (not as well tested) from the
    66	Github master branch:
    67	
    68	    conda create -n <env_name> python
    69	    conda activate <env_name>
    70	    pip install git+https://github.com/spacetelescope/jwst
    71

    73	### Installing a DMS Operational Build
    74	
    75	There may be occasions where an exact copy of an operational DMS build is
    76	desired (e.g. for validation testing or debugging operational issues).
    77	We package releases for DMS builds via environment snapshots that specify the
    78	exact versions of all packages to be installed.
    79	
    80	To install a particular DMS build, consult the
    81	[Software vs DMS build version map](https://github.com/spacetelescope/jwst#software-vs-dms-build-version-map)
    82	table shown below to determine the correct jwst tag. For example, to install the
    83	version of `jwst` used in DMS build 9.0, use jwst tag 1.8.2. The overall
    84	procedure is similar to the 3-step process outlined in the previous section, but the
    85	details of each command vary, due to the use of environment snapshot files that specify
    86	all of the particular packages to install. Also note that different snapshot files are
    87	used for Linux and Mac OS systems.
    88	
    89	Linux:
    90	
    91	    conda create -n jwstdp-1.8.2 --file https://ssb.stsci.edu/releases/jwstdp/1.8.2/conda_python_stable-deps.txt
    92	    conda activate jwstdp-1.8.2
    93	    pip install -r https://ssb.stsci.edu/releases/jwstdp/1.8.2/reqs_stable-deps.txt
    94	
    95	MacOS:
    96	
    97	    conda create -n jwstdp-1.8.2 --file https://ssb.stsci.edu/releases/jwstdp/1.8.2/conda_python_macos-stable-deps.txt
    98	    conda activate jwstdp-1.8.2
    99	    pip install -r https://ssb.stsci.edu/releases/jwstdp/1.8.2/reqs_macos-stable-deps.txt
   100

   104	The installation procedures may change from time to time, so consulting the

   109	### Installing for Developers
   110	
   111	If you want to be able to work on and test the source code with the `jwst` package,
   112	the high-level procedure to do this is to first create a conda environment using
   113	the same procedures outlined above, but then install your personal copy of the
   114	code overtop of the original code in that environment. Again, this should be done
   115	in a separate conda environment from any existing environments that you may have
   116	already installed with released versions of the `jwst` package.
   117	
   118	As usual, the first two steps are to create and activate an environment:
   119	
   120	    conda create -n <env_name> python
   121	    conda activate <env_name>
   122	
   123	To install your own copy of the code into that environment, you first need to
   124	fork and clone the `jwst` repo:
   125	
   126	    cd <where you want to put the repo>
   127	    git clone https://github.com/<your_github_username>/jwst.git
   128	    cd jwst
   129	
   130	*Note: `python setup.py install` and `python setup.py develop` commands do not work.*
   131	
   132	Install from your local checked-out copy as an "editable" install:
   133	
   134	    pip install -e .
   135	
   136	If you want to run the unit or regression tests and/or build the docs, you can make
   137	sure those dependencies are installed too:
   138	
   139	    pip install -e ".[test]"
   140	    pip install -e ".[docs]"
   141	    pip install -e ".[test,docs]"
   142	
   143	Need other useful packages in your development environment?
   144	
   145	    pip install ipython jupyter matplotlib pylint

   148	## Calibration References Data System (CRDS) Setup
   149	
   150	**Note: As of November 10, 2022, the process of deprecating the CRDS PUB Server will start.
   151	For details, refer to the [CRDS PUB Server Freeze
   152	and Deprecation page](https://jwst-pipeline.readthedocs.io/en/stable/jwst/pub_deprecation.html#pub-deprecation)**
   153	
   154	
   155	CRDS is the system that manages the reference files needed to run the pipeline.
   156	For details about CRDS, see the [User's
   157	Guide](https://jwst-crds.stsci.edu/static/users_guide/index.html)
   158	
   159	The JWST CRDS server is available at  https://jwst-crds.stsci.edu
   160	
   161	It supports the automatic processing pipeline at STScI.
   162	Inside the STScI network, the same server is used by the pipeline by default with no modifications.
   163	To run the pipeline outside the STScI network, CRDS must be configured by setting
   164	two environment variables:
   165	
   166	    export CRDS_PATH=<locally-accessable-path>/crds_cache/jwst_ops
   167	    export CRDS_SERVER_URL=https://jwst-crds.stsci.edu
   168	
   169	
   170	``<locally-accessable-path>`` can be any the user has permissions to use, such as `$HOME`.
   171	Expect to use upwards of 200GB of disk space to cache the latest couple of contexts.
